analysis.one_liner: Creates a national paid family and medical leave insurance program for workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2025 with 39 Senate supporters, all Democrats or independents; it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sits with no hearing or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAMILY Act would create a national paid family and medical leave insurance program, run through the Social Security Administration. Workers who need time off — for a new child, their own serious illness, or to care for a family member with a serious health condition, or to deal with domestic violence or sexual assault — would receive a monthly check replacing part of their wages: 85% of earnings at the low end, sliding to 50% for higher earners, with a floor of $580 and a cap of $4,000 per month. It would be funded by a small new payroll tax (0.4%, split between workers and employers) and cover employees and self-employed people alike. It would also make it illegal for an employer to fire or retaliate against someone for taking the leave, and would require the employer to hold the person's job or an equivalent one.
analysis.who_benefits: All workers and self-employed people who need time off for a new child, their own serious illness, a family member's serious health condition, or safety needs after domestic violence or sexual assault. Low-wage workers benefit most in relative terms, since the benefit replaces up to 85% of their earnings and they are the least likely to have employer-paid leave today. Workers in states with existing paid-leave programs also benefit, because the federal government would reimburse their states' benefit and administrative costs.

how_it_helps.text: Provides monthly cash benefits for up to 12 months of leave for a new child, a serious health condition of the worker or a broad circle of family members, or needs arising from domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

Replaces wages progressively — 85% of earnings at the lowest income tier, sliding to 50% at the top — with a monthly minimum of $580 and maximum of $4,000, so the benefit is most generous relative to income for the lowest-paid workers.

Makes it unlawful for an employer to fire or retaliate against a worker for taking the leave, requires job restoration to the same or an equivalent position, keeps employer health coverage in place during leave, and creates a rebuttable presumption that adverse action within 12 months of leave is retaliation.

Covers self-employed workers, includes chosen and extended family in the definition of who can be cared for, and lets states with their own paid-leave programs (such as California, New York, and New Jersey) keep their programs while receiving federal grants to cover their costs.
Applies to domestic violence and sexual assault survivors specifically, covering relocation, legal proceedings, counseling, and school or care changes for the victim or family member.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and employers, through a new 0.4% payroll tax on wages (and self-employment income) split evenly between them. Higher earners also pay in that their benefits are capped, and taxpayers generally bear the administrative cost of the new Social Security Administration office.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and employers via payroll tax

drawbacks.text: The program is funded by a new payroll tax on both employees and employers, which comes out of workers' paychecks and business budgets — an honest supporter must acknowledge this cost, though employers currently pay the costs of unpaid leave and turnover when workers quit after a birth or illness.

It creates a large new federal entitlement administered by the Social Security Administration, and the bill's own reporting provisions acknowledge that application processing speed and possible delays are a concern to be studied by the Government Accountability Office.
Benefits replace at most a share of wages and cap at $4,000 per month, so higher earners taking leave would see a bigger pay cut than the headline 85% replacement rate suggests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete: a national floor of paid leave for a life event every working family eventually faces, replacing about 2-3 months of typical earnings. The costs are real: a new payroll tax on every working person and employer during a period when payroll tax burden and trust-fund finances are already contested, and a permanent new administrative program. Versions of this bill have stalled in prior Congresses, and no Republican cosponsors have signed on, so the main practical cost of supporting it now may be political rather than fiscal — but the bill as written has not advanced even to a committee hearing in this Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor action — the usual path by which bills die quietly.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 16, 2025 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance, the Senate committee that handles Social Security and tax matters.
No further action has been taken since the referral: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action appear in the record.
All 38 cosponsors are Democrats or the independent who caucuses with them; no Republican has signed on.

The bill itself is detailed and complete, not a placeholder — it specifies benefit formulas, administrative structure, anti-retaliation protections, and how it coordinates with existing state paid-leave programs.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and higher-income households are spared a new payroll tax so far, and no worker has gained the leave benefit the bill would have provided. The bill's supporters retain an introduced bill they can point to, but no worker has received anything from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers spared a new payroll tax; workers gained nothing

for.name: Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 38 Senate cosponsors.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill; as the senior Democrat on the committee of referral, he is the member best positioned to push it to a hearing.

for.name: 38 Senate cosponsors (37 Democrats, 1 independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including the Senate party leader Chuck Schumer.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors are Democrats or the independent who caucuses with Democrats; no Republican has sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and Republicans control the Senate and its Finance Committee in this Congress.

industries.note: Employers pay half of the new 0.4% payroll tax and must hold jobs open, maintain health coverage, and refrain from retaliation during leave. Small businesses bear the same per-employee cost as large ones, though the benefit removes the burden of financing leave themselves.

Workers pay the other half of the payroll tax on wages, and self-employed people pay it on self-employment income. In exchange they receive an insurance benefit they can draw on for their own or a family member's serious health event or a new child.

industries.industry: State paid-family-leave programs and the insurers/administrators serving them
industries.note: States with existing paid-leave programs keep running them and receive federal grants covering their benefit and administrative costs, locking in the state systems and the employer-provided plans and insurers that administer them within those states.

industries.industry: Temporary staffing and gig-adjacent labor intermediaries
industries.note: The program reduces the pressure on workers to accept any job rather than take leave, which can increase the cost and difficulty of filling short-term roles; the effect on this sector is real but smaller than on direct employers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Finance Committee with no hearing or vote scheduled, and with no Republican cosponsors in a chamber where legislation generally needs 60 votes to advance. First-time referrals of social insurance bills with single-party support rarely reach the floor. The most realistic path is that the bill remains a marker for a future Congress or serves as a template if paid leave is negotiated into a larger package; it is unlikely to become law this Congress as introduced.
